title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
text:
A poor old fisherman went down to the sea every day and cast his net exactly four times. One day the first three casts brought up a dead donkey, a jar full of mud and a heap of broken pots. On the fourth cast he pulled up a copper jar, sealed with lead and stamped with the seal of King Solomon.

He opened it, hoping to sell it, and smoke poured out and rose to the sky, then gathered into a gigantic jinni. The jinni told the fisherman to choose how he wanted to die. Solomon had shut him in that jar centuries ago, he explained. During the first hundred years he had sworn to make his rescuer rich. During the next he swore to open the treasures of the earth for him. Then he swore to grant three wishes. When no one came, he grew furious and vowed to kill whoever freed him.

The fisherman thought quickly. He said he simply could not believe that such an enormous being had ever fit inside such a small jar. He would never believe it unless he saw it with his own eyes.

Stung, the jinni turned back into smoke and poured himself into the jar to prove it. At once the fisherman jammed the lead stopper back on. Now it was the jinni who pleaded, and he was freed again only after swearing an oath to do the fisherman no harm.
lesson: A powerful opponent's pride can be his weak point. Questioning what someone boasts about can lead him to step right into the trap.
location: Medieval Middle East (Persian and Arabic tradition)
caveat: Details of the first three casts and of the ending differ between versions.
